topics.title: Production Readiness Checklist
topics.summary: What to configure before real users arrive: NODE_ENV, config, security, logging, limits, health and shutdown.
topics.description:
"It works on my machine" is not production. Run through this checklist before every launch.

### Runtime and config
* Use an active **LTS** Node version, pinned (`.nvmrc`, `engines`, Docker tag)
* Set `NODE_ENV=production` (Express and many libraries disable debug features and enable caching)
* All configuration from **environment variables**; fail fast when something is missing
* `npm ci --omit=dev` so devDependencies are not installed
* Never run as root (in containers use the `node` user)

### Security
* HTTPS everywhere, HSTS, `helmet`, strict CORS allow-list
* Secrets in a secret manager, never in git or images
* Rate limiting, body size limits, input validation
* `npm audit` clean (or accepted), dependencies updated
* `trust proxy` configured behind a load balancer
* Hide stack traces and `X-Powered-By`

### Reliability
* **Graceful shutdown** on SIGTERM
* **Health endpoints** (`/health`, `/ready`)
* Timeouts for every outgoing call (database, HTTP)
* Process supervisor/orchestrator restarts crashes (PM2, systemd, Docker, Kubernetes)
* Connection pools sized for your database limits
* Uncaught exception and rejection handlers: log and exit

### Observability
* Structured logs to stdout with request ids
* Error tracking (Sentry), metrics and uptime checks
* Alerts for error rate, latency, memory and disk

### Data
* Database **migrations** are automated and tested
* **Backups** exist and restoring has been practised
* Indexes for the real queries

### Performance
* Compression (gzip/brotli, usually at the proxy), caching headers, a CDN for static files
* Run on all cores (cluster/PM2/replicas)
* Load tested at expected traffic

### Release process
CI runs lint and tests; deploys are automated, repeatable and **reversible** (rollback plan, previous image kept).
keyPoints: Pin an LTS Node version and set NODE_ENV=production
Configuration and secrets come from the environment
Health checks, graceful shutdown and restarts make the app resilient
Structured logs, error tracking and alerts are mandatory
Automate migrations and test your backups and rollbacks
pitfalls: Deploying with NODE_ENV unset (development behaviour in production)
No timeouts on outgoing requests
Backups that were never restored in practice

examples.title: Start-up guard rails
examples.explanation: keepAliveTimeout above the load balancer idle timeout avoids sporadic 502 errors.

interview.a: Libraries use it to enable optimisations and disable development behaviour: Express caches views and hides detailed errors, and many packages skip debug code. It is a convention, so your own code can also branch on it.

interview.q: Why set keepAliveTimeout higher than the load balancer idle timeout?
interview.a: If Node closes an idle connection before the balancer does, the balancer may send a request on a connection that is just closing, causing intermittent 502 errors. Keeping Node's timeout larger avoids that race.

topics.title: Docker for Node.js
topics.summary: Package your app in a small, secure image: multi-stage builds, layer caching, non-root user, signals and compose.
topics.description:
**Docker** packages your app with its exact runtime so it runs the same on every machine and server.

### Key terms
* **Image**: the read-only package (OS layer, Node, your code)
* **Container**: a running instance of an image
* **Dockerfile**: the build recipe; **.dockerignore** excludes files from the build context
* **Compose**: define multi-container setups (app + database + redis)

### Best practices
1. **Small base**: `node:22-slim` or `node:22-alpine` (alpine uses musl; some native modules prefer slim)
2. **Layer caching**: copy `package*.json` and run `npm ci` **before** copying source, so dependency layers are reused
3. **Multi-stage build**: build (TypeScript, bundling) in one stage, copy only results into a lean runtime stage
4. `npm ci --omit=dev` in the final stage
5. **Run as non-root**: `USER node`
6. `ENV NODE_ENV=production`
7. Use the **exec form** `CMD ["node", "server.js"]` so Node is PID 1 and receives SIGTERM (not `npm start`)
8. `HEALTHCHECK` or orchestrator probes
9. `.dockerignore`: `node_modules`, `.git`, `.env`, logs, tests
10. Pin versions; scan images (`docker scout`, Trivy)

### Config and secrets
Pass settings at run time: `docker run --env-file .env -p 3000:3000 app`. Do not bake secrets into the image or `COPY .env`.

### Useful commands
`docker build -t shop-api .`, `docker run -p 3000:3000 shop-api`, `docker logs -f`, `docker compose up -d`, `docker exec -it <id> sh`.

### Development
Compose with a bind mount and `node --watch` gives live reload inside a container (`docker compose watch` also syncs files).
keyPoints: Copy package files and install before copying source to use layer caching
Multi-stage builds keep images small
Run as the non-root node user with NODE_ENV=production
Use CMD in exec form so signals reach Node
Never bake secrets into images; use .dockerignore
pitfalls: COPY . . before npm ci (cache busted on every code change)
Using npm start as the container command (SIGTERM lost)
Running as root and shipping devDependencies

examples.title: Dockerfile (multi-stage)
examples.code:
# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1
FROM node:22-slim AS deps
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --omit=dev

FROM node:22-slim AS build
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci
COPY . .
RUN npm run build            # tsc / bundler; remove if you have no build step

FROM node:22-slim AS runtime
ENV NODE_ENV=production
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=deps  /app/node_modules ./node_modules
COPY --from=build /app/dist ./dist
COPY package.json ./
USER node
EXPOSE 3000
HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s --timeout=3s --start-period=10s \
  CMD node -e "fetch('http://127.0.0.1:3000/health').then(r=>process.exit(r.ok?0:1)).catch(()=>process.exit(1))"
CMD ["node", "dist/server.js"]
examples.explanation: The final image has production dependencies and compiled output only.

examples.title: .dockerignore and docker-compose.yml
examples.code:
# .dockerignore
node_modules
.git
.env
*.log
coverage
dist

# docker-compose.yml
services:
  api:
    build: .
    ports: ["3000:3000"]
    env_file: .env
    environment:
      DATABASE_URL: postgres://app:secret@db:5432/shop
    depends_on:
      db:
        condition: service_healthy
    restart: unless-stopped
  db:
    image: postgres:16
    environment:
      POSTGRES_USER: app
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: secret
      POSTGRES_DB: shop
    volumes: [pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data]
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U app -d shop"]
      interval: 5s
      retries: 10
volumes:
  pgdata:
examples.explanation: Inside the compose network the database host name is the service name db.

interview.q: Why copy package.json before the source code in a Dockerfile?
interview.a: Docker caches each layer. Dependencies change rarely, so copying package files and running npm ci first lets Docker reuse that cached layer when only source files change, making rebuilds fast.

interview.q: Why use CMD ["node", "server.js"] instead of npm start?
interview.a: Exec form makes Node the main process (PID 1) so it receives SIGTERM and can shut down gracefully. npm start adds a wrapper process that often does not forward signals.

topics.title: nginx as a Reverse Proxy
topics.summary: Put nginx in front of Node for TLS, compression, static files, load balancing and WebSocket support.
topics.description:
A **reverse proxy** sits between the internet and your Node app. Clients talk to nginx, and nginx forwards requests to Node on a private port.

### Why use one
* **TLS termination** and automatic certificates (certbot / Let's Encrypt)
* Serves **static files** and caches far faster than Node
* **Compression**, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3
* **Load balancing** across several Node instances
* Rate limiting, request size limits, security headers
* Buffers slow clients so Node is not tied up (slowloris protection)
* One server can host several apps by domain name

### Typical config
Map a domain to `http://127.0.0.1:3000`, forward the original host and client IP via headers, and redirect HTTP to HTTPS.

### Headers Node needs
`X-Forwarded-For`, `X-Forwarded-Proto`, `X-Forwarded-Host`. In Express set `app.set('trust proxy', 1)` so `req.ip`, `req.protocol` and `Secure` cookies work.

### WebSockets and SSE
WebSockets need `proxy_http_version 1.1;` plus `Upgrade` and `Connection` headers. For server-sent events set `proxy_buffering off;` and a long `proxy_read_timeout`.

### Operations
`sudo nginx -t` tests the config, `sudo systemctl reload nginx` applies it without downtime. Logs are in `/var/log/nginx/`.

### Alternatives
**Caddy** (automatic HTTPS with a tiny config), **Traefik** (container aware), HAProxy, cloud load balancers (ALB), and platform routers on Render or Railway.
keyPoints: nginx terminates TLS, serves static files and forwards the rest to Node
Pass X-Forwarded-* headers and enable trust proxy in Express
WebSockets require Upgrade headers; SSE needs buffering off
nginx -t before reload; use certbot for certificates
Caddy is a simpler alternative with automatic HTTPS
pitfalls: Forgetting trust proxy, so every client appears as 127.0.0.1
Missing WebSocket upgrade headers
Default 1 MB client_max_body_size blocking uploads

examples.title: nginx server block
examples.explanation: Enable with a symlink into sites-enabled, then run sudo nginx -t and sudo systemctl reload nginx.

examples.title: Certificates and Express setting
examples.code:
sudo apt install nginx certbot python3-certbot-nginx
sudo certbot --nginx -d example.com -d www.example.com    # gets and renews certificates
sudo nginx -t && sudo systemctl reload nginx

# in your Node app
# app.set('trust proxy', 1);
examples.explanation: certbot installs a timer that renews certificates automatically.

interview.a: nginx handles TLS, static files, compression, buffering and load balancing efficiently, protects Node from slow clients and lets you run several apps and scale instances without exposing Node directly.

interview.q: What breaks if you forget trust proxy?
interview.a: Express sees the proxy as the client: req.ip is 127.0.0.1, req.protocol is http, secure cookies are not set and IP-based rate limits treat all users as one.

topics.title: CI/CD with GitHub Actions
topics.summary: Automate lint, test, build and deployment on every push, with secrets, caching and environments.
topics.description:
**Continuous Integration** runs checks on every change; **Continuous Delivery/Deployment** ships passing builds automatically. Together they make releases boring and safe.

### Stages of a Node pipeline
1. **Install**: `npm ci` (with dependency cache)
2. **Lint and typecheck**: `npm run lint`, `tsc --noEmit`
3. **Test**: unit and integration tests, with service containers (Postgres, Redis) if needed
4. **Audit**: `npm audit --omit=dev`
5. **Build**: compile TypeScript or build a Docker image
6. **Publish**: push the image to a registry (GHCR, Docker Hub, ECR)
7. **Deploy**: SSH to a server, call a platform deploy hook, update Kubernetes
8. **Smoke test**: hit `/health` after deployment; roll back on failure

### GitHub Actions basics
Workflows are YAML files in `.github/workflows/`. Triggers: `push`, `pull_request`, `schedule`, `workflow_dispatch`. A **job** runs on a runner (`ubuntu-latest`) and consists of **steps** (`uses:` an action or `run:` a command). **Secrets** (Settings, Secrets) are exposed as `${{ secrets.NAME }}`. **Environments** add approvals for production.

### Good practices
* Protect `main`: require passing checks and reviews
* Use the `matrix` strategy to test several Node versions
* Cache with `actions/setup-node` (`cache: npm`)
* Keep deployments **idempotent** and reversible; tag images with the git SHA
* Never print secrets; grant jobs minimal permissions
* Run deployments only from `main` (or tags), after tests pass

### Hosting integrations
Render, Railway, Vercel and Fly.io deploy on git push directly; Actions still handle tests before merging.
keyPoints: CI runs lint, tests and builds on every push or pull request
CD deploys passing builds automatically and reversibly
Use secrets and environments for credentials and approvals
Tag Docker images with the commit SHA
Protect main with required status checks
pitfalls: Deploying without running tests
Echoing secrets in logs
Non-reversible deployments with no rollback plan

examples.title: Test and deploy workflow
examples.code:
# .github/workflows/deploy.yml
name: CI/CD
on:
  push: { branches: [main] }
  pull_request:

jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    services:
      postgres:
        image: postgres:16
        env: { POSTGRES_PASSWORD: test, POSTGRES_DB: app_test }
        ports: ['5432:5432']
        options: >-
          --health-cmd "pg_isready -U postgres" --health-interval 5s --health-retries 10
    env:
      DATABASE_URL: postgres://postgres:test@localhost:5432/app_test
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with: { node-version: 22, cache: npm }
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm run lint
      - run: npm test
      - run: npm audit --omit=dev --audit-level=high

  deploy:
    needs: test
    if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: production
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Deploy over SSH
        uses: appleboy/ssh-action@v1
        with:
          host: ${{ secrets.SSH_HOST }}
          username: deploy
          key: ${{ secrets.SSH_KEY }}
          script: |
            cd /var/www/myapp
            git pull origin main
            npm ci --omit=dev
            npm run migrate
            pm2 reload ecosystem.config.cjs --env production
      - name: Smoke test
        run: curl --fail --retry 5 --retry-delay 3 https://example.com/health
examples.explanation: The deploy job runs only after tests pass on main, then verifies the live health endpoint.

interview.q: What is the difference between continuous delivery and continuous deployment?
interview.a: Continuous delivery keeps every build ready to release but a person approves the production release. Continuous deployment releases every passing change to production automatically.

interview.q: Why use npm ci in CI pipelines?
interview.a: It installs exactly what the lock file defines, fails if package.json and the lock file differ and starts from a clean node_modules, giving reproducible builds.

topics.title: Hosting: Render, Railway, VPS and More
topics.summary: Compare platform-as-a-service, containers and a plain VPS, and the steps to deploy to each.
topics.description:
Where you host depends on budget, control and traffic.

### Options
| Type | Examples | Pros | Cons |
|---|---|---|---|
| **PaaS** | Render, Railway, Fly.io, Heroku, Koyeb | Deploy from git, HTTPS and scaling included | Costs grow, less control |
| **Serverless / edge** | Vercel, AWS Lambda, Cloudflare Workers | Scale to zero, pay per use | Cold starts, execution limits, different model |
| **Containers** | AWS ECS/Fargate, Google Cloud Run, Azure Container Apps | Portable, scalable | More concepts |
| **Kubernetes** | EKS, GKE, DOKS | Powerful orchestration | Complex |
| **VPS** | DigitalOcean, Hetzner, Linode, AWS EC2 | Cheap, full control | You manage OS, security, updates |

### Deploying to a PaaS (Render/Railway)
1. Push your code to GitHub
2. Create a **Web Service** from the repository
3. Build command `npm ci` (and `npm run build`), start command `npm start`
4. Add **environment variables** in the dashboard (DATABASE_URL, JWT_SECRET)
5. **Listen on `process.env.PORT`** and host `0.0.0.0`
6. Add a managed database; set a health check path
7. Every push to `main` redeploys

Free tiers may sleep when idle (first request is slow) and have ephemeral disks: do not store uploads locally.

### Deploying to a VPS
1. Create a server, add an SSH key, disable password login
2. Create a non-root user, enable a firewall (`ufw allow 22,80,443`)
3. Install Node (nvm or NodeSource), nginx and certbot
4. Clone the repo, `npm ci --omit=dev`, create the `.env`
5. Run with PM2 or systemd; configure nginx; get TLS certificates
6. Set up backups and updates (`unattended-upgrades`)

### Databases
Use managed databases (Neon, Supabase, MongoDB Atlas, PlanetScale, Render/Railway Postgres) so backups and updates are handled for you.
keyPoints: PaaS (Render, Railway) is the fastest way to deploy from git
A VPS gives control but you manage security and updates
Always listen on process.env.PORT and 0.0.0.0
Use environment variables and managed databases
Do not rely on local disk for persistent data on PaaS
pitfalls: Hard-coding the port, so the platform health check fails
Binding to localhost only inside a container or PaaS
Storing uploads on ephemeral disks

examples.title: Platform-ready start-up and scripts
examples.explanation: Platforms inject PORT and call npm run build then npm start.

examples.title: First-time VPS setup
examples.code:
ssh root@203.0.113.10
adduser deploy && usermod -aG sudo deploy
ufw allow OpenSSH && ufw allow 80 && ufw allow 443 && ufw enable
# as deploy user:
curl -fsSL https://deb.nodesource.com/setup_22.x | sudo -E bash - && sudo apt install -y nodejs nginx
sudo npm i -g pm2
git clone https://github.com/you/app.git && cd app && npm ci --omit=dev
cp .env.example .env && nano .env
pm2 start ecosystem.config.cjs --env production && pm2 save && pm2 startup
examples.explanation: Then configure nginx and certbot as shown in the reverse proxy topic.

interview.q: Why must you read the port from process.env.PORT on platforms like Render?
interview.a: The platform assigns the port at runtime and routes traffic to it. If your app listens on a hard-coded port, the platform cannot reach it and the deploy fails health checks.

interview.q: What are the downsides of a VPS compared to a PaaS?
interview.a: You must secure and patch the OS, set up TLS, process management, backups and monitoring yourself, which costs time but gives more control and a lower price at scale.

topics.title: Monitoring, Metrics and Error Tracking
topics.summary: See what production is doing: structured logs, metrics, uptime checks, error tracking (Sentry) and alerts.
topics.description:
You cannot fix what you cannot see. Monitoring answers: **Is it up? Is it fast? What is failing? Who is affected?**

### The three pillars
| Pillar | What | Tools |
|---|---|---|
| **Logs** | Discrete events | pino to stdout, Loki, ELK, Datadog, CloudWatch, Better Stack |
| **Metrics** | Numbers over time | Prometheus + Grafana, Datadog, `prom-client` |
| **Traces** | A request's path across services | OpenTelemetry, Jaeger, Datadog APM |

### What to measure (RED and USE)
* **Rate**: requests per second
* **Errors**: 5xx rate and error counts
* **Duration**: latency percentiles (p50, p95, p99)
* Resources: CPU, memory (`heapUsed`, RSS), **event loop lag**, open handles, DB pool usage, queue depth

### Error tracking
**Sentry** (or Rollbar, Bugsnag) captures exceptions with stack traces, request data, user and release version, groups duplicates and alerts you. Initialise it first in your app and add the Express error handler. Upload source maps for TypeScript or bundled code.

### Uptime and alerts
External pingers (UptimeRobot, Better Stack, Pingdom) call `/health` from outside. Alert on symptoms users feel: high error rate, high p95 latency, failing health checks, low disk, memory growth. Avoid alert fatigue: every alert should be actionable.

### prom-client example idea
Expose `GET /metrics` with a default metrics collector plus an `http_request_duration_seconds` histogram. Prometheus scrapes it; Grafana draws dashboards.

### Release tracking
Tag errors with a version or git SHA so you see which deploy introduced a problem, and correlate logs with a **request id**.
keyPoints: Logs, metrics and traces answer different questions
Track request rate, errors, latency percentiles and event loop lag
Sentry-style error tracking groups exceptions with context
External uptime checks plus actionable alerts
Tag releases and correlate by request id
pitfalls: Only monitoring CPU, ignoring latency and errors
Alerts that nobody acts on (alert fatigue)
No release or request id on errors

examples.title: Prometheus metrics endpoint
examples.explanation: Use the route pattern (/users/:id), not the raw URL, as a label to avoid millions of label values.

examples.title: Sentry setup
examples.explanation: Every unhandled error is sent to Sentry with the request context and release.

interview.q: What are the three pillars of observability?
interview.a: Logs (events), metrics (aggregated numbers over time) and traces (the path of a single request through services). Together they let you detect, locate and understand problems.

interview.q: Why is event loop lag a useful metric for Node?
interview.a: It shows how long callbacks wait because the single thread is busy. Rising lag means blocking code or CPU saturation, and it correlates with slow responses for all users.

topics.title: Health Checks and Zero-Downtime Deploys
topics.summary: Liveness and readiness endpoints, load balancer integration and rolling deploys that never drop requests.
topics.description:
Load balancers and orchestrators need to know **whether to send traffic to an instance** and **whether to restart it**. Health endpoints answer.

### Two kinds
| Probe | Question | On failure |
|---|---|---|
| **Liveness** `/health` | Is the process alive and not stuck? | Restart the instance |
| **Readiness** `/ready` | Can it serve traffic right now (DB connected, warmed up, not shutting down)? | Stop sending traffic, keep the process |

Keep liveness **cheap and dependency free** (return 200). Checking the database in liveness can cause restart storms when the database blips. Readiness may check the database and cache with short timeouts.

### Rolling deploy flow
1. New instance starts and becomes **ready**
2. Load balancer adds it to the pool
3. Old instance receives SIGTERM, flips readiness to **503** and finishes in-flight requests (`server.close`)
4. It exits; the next instance is replaced

Repeat one by one. With PM2 use `pm2 reload`; with Kubernetes `RollingUpdate`; with Docker Compose use health checks and multiple replicas behind a proxy.

### Kubernetes hints
`livenessProbe`, `readinessProbe` and `startupProbe` with `httpGet`. `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` should exceed your shutdown deadline. A short `preStop` sleep (5 s) lets endpoints deregister first.

### Database migrations
Make schema changes **backward compatible** (expand, deploy, contract), so old and new versions run together during the rollout.

### Version endpoint
`/version` returns the git SHA, helping verify what is deployed.

### Rollback
Keep the previous image or release. Roll back first, debug later; make the rollback a single command.
keyPoints: Liveness checks the process, readiness checks it can serve traffic
Keep liveness free of external dependencies
Flip readiness off on SIGTERM before closing the server
Rolling deploys replace instances one by one
Use backward-compatible migrations and keep a rollback path
pitfalls: Making the liveness probe depend on the database
Not failing readiness during shutdown, so traffic hits a closing server
Breaking migrations that old instances cannot tolerate

examples.title: Health, readiness and shutdown
examples.explanation: The 5-second delay lets the load balancer remove the instance before connections are closed.

examples.title: Kubernetes probes
examples.code:
containers:
  - name: api
    image: ghcr.io/you/api:3f2b6c1
    ports: [{ containerPort: 3000 }]
    livenessProbe:
      httpGet: { path: /health, port: 3000 }
      periodSeconds: 10
      failureThreshold: 3
    readinessProbe:
      httpGet: { path: /ready, port: 3000 }
      periodSeconds: 5
    lifecycle:
      preStop:
        exec: { command: ["sleep", "5"] }
terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 30
examples.explanation: Kubernetes stops routing to the pod when readiness fails and restarts it when liveness fails repeatedly.

interview.a: Liveness tells the platform whether to restart a stuck process; readiness tells the load balancer whether to send traffic. A starting or shutting-down app can be live but not ready.

interview.q: How do you deploy without dropping requests?
interview.a: Start new instances and wait for readiness, then drain old ones: fail readiness on SIGTERM, stop accepting connections, finish in-flight requests, then exit, repeating gradually (rolling update).
